regions.label: Meno-Lite-0.1 model description
regions.description: Describes the model's origin, continued pre-training and supervised fine-tuning, training tasks, context-oriented instruction design, context window, tokenizer efficiency, deployment, and public model card.
regions.visible_text: Meno-Lite-0.1 (Bondarenko et al., 2026) is derived from RuadaptQwen2.5-7B-Lite-Beta (Tikhomirov and Chernyshev, 2025) through continued pre-training (1.3B tokens, Russian+English educational/scientific texts) and supervised fine-tuning (50M tokens) covering NEREL-based extraction (Loukachevitch et al., 2021), multi-hop QA (Tang and Yang, 2024; Katsis et al., 2025), and query logs. The critical distinction from general-purpose LLMs: instructions teach the model to use context rather than recall facts—investing compute in language skills, not world knowledge. Key properties: 128K context window (passkey retrieval 0.98 at 128K), 47% better tokenizer efficiency than vanilla Qwen2.5 on Russian text (3.77 vs. 2.57 chars/token), and single-consumer-GPU deployment via vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023). The model and training details are documented in the public model card at https://huggingface.co/bond005/meno-lite-0.1.

regions.label: GraphRAG-Bench cross-over results
regions.description: Reports that HippoRAG 2 leads on factoid levels, while RAGU's relative performance improves as tasks require broader synthesis and leads on Creative Generation and Coverage. It also states that LightRAG is weakest at every level.
regions.visible_text: Table 1 and Figure 3 reveal a cross-over. On the two factoid levels, HippoRAG 2 leads: its personalized PageRank pins down single facts (AC 72.4 vs. 54.2 for RAGU on Fact Retrieval, Δ = −18.2 pp). As tasks demand broad synthesis rather than chain-following, the gap closes monotonically—Complex Reasoning (−14.7 pp), Contextual Summarize (−0.9 pp, parity)—and reverses on Creative Generation, where RAGU wins AC (59.0 vs. 56.9) and Faithfulness (34.2 vs. 26.6). On Coverage, the metric that directly rewards retrieving all relevant material, RAGU leads throughout (57.4 vs. 34.7 on Creative Generation). LightRAG is weakest at every level, confirming that single-pass free-form extraction produces a structurally poorer graph than typed multi-step consolidation.

regions.label: Retrieval and ablation findings
regions.description: Reports Evidence Recall, explains HippoRAG 2's factoid accuracy, summarizes ablations, and begins a statement about robustness across extraction-model sizes. The final sentence continues beyond the visible page area.
regions.visible_text: Retrieval results confirm the mechanism: RAGU attains the highest Evidence Recall at every factoid level (84 vs. ≤76% for competitors), directly supporting the consolidation hypothesis. That HippoRAG 2 nonetheless wins factoid AC despite lower Evidence Recall reflects the precision of its chain traversal on single-fact queries. Ablation results (Appendix B) show that the ICL and validation toggles each shift AC by at most ~1.5 pp, so the gap to competitors cannot be attributed to those options; it reflects the aggregate effect of RAGU’s structural choices. Figure 3: Cross-over by task complexity on GraphRAG-Bench (Medical). All three systems use Meno-Lite-0.1 (7 B) as the index LLM and gpt-4o-mini for answer generation. (a) Answer Correctness: RAGU trails HippoRAG 2 on Fact Retrieval, but the gap closes and RAGU leads on Creative Generation. 3.3 Multi-Hop QA Results
These benchmarks are pure factoid QA with short gold answers, for which answer format strongly affects overlap-based metrics. We therefore report two answer-generation protocols (Table 2): (a) each system’s default verbose prompt, and (b) a terse prompt that forces a single direct answer. HippoRAG 2 appears in both panels unchanged because its default prompt already emits terse output, making it a format anchor; NaiveRAG is RAGU’s NaiveSearchEngine and therefore shares our generation prompt.

Under the verbose protocol (a), HippoRAG 2 dominates every column (AC up to 74.1 vs. 56.0 for

regions.label: Section 3.3 right-column continuation
regions.description: Discusses format effects, controlled-format comparisons on BioASQ, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and MuSiQue, and concludes that the systems have complementary strengths. The final sentence is cut off.
regions.visible_text:
RAGU on BioASQ). This gap, however, is largely a format artifact: verbose answers mismatch the terse gold references, depressing both ROUGE-L (12 vs. 49) and Answer Correctness. Once format is controlled (b), the picture changes substantially. RAGU ties (and slightly exceeds HippoRAG 2 on BioASQ AC (72.9 vs. 72.4) and closes the 2Wiki-MultiHopQA gap from −19.3 pp to −5.5 pp (58.0 vs. 63.5). analysis.title: ToolAtlas overview page: memory bootstrapping, capability exploration, and dynamic memory traversal
analysis.summary: Observed: A research-paper page dominated by Figure 2, which presents the ToolAtlas workflow in three numbered stages: (1) Memory Bootstrapping, (2) Capability Exploration, and (3) Dynamic Memory Traversal. The diagram shows seed tasks and verified tool rollouts being converted into a three-part memory architecture containing trace, capability, and strategy graphs. The lower half contains two-column technical prose defining the Tool-Capability Graph and Tool-Strategy Graph and begins Section 3.2, “Capability Exploration.” Interpretation: The page explains how ToolAtlas builds and expands reusable tool-side memory, then retrieves traces, strategies, and tool information to guide a user agent.

Stage 2 uses the current graph to propose capability explorations that test tool boundaries and affordances, then writes verified outcomes back to the graph. Stage 3 traverses the graph at inference time and summarizes the retrieved traces, tool entries, and strategies into task-conditioned guidance for a user agent.

regions.label: Figure 2 caption
regions.description: Observed: Caption summarizes all three ToolAtlas stages and the role of the memory graph.
regions.visible_text: Figure 2: Overview of ToolAtlas. Stage 1 bootstraps a tool-side memory graph from seed tasks and verified rollouts, where Memory Induction converts raw trajectories into tool memory graph. Stage 2 uses the current graph to propose capability explorations that test tool boundaries and affordances, then writes verified outcomes back to the graph. Stage 3 traverses the graph at inference time and summarizes the retrieved traces, tool entries, and strategies into task-conditioned guidance for a user agent.

regions.label: Tool-Capability Graph subsection text
regions.description: Observed: The prose defines a graph whose nodes are tools and whose inter-tool edges summarize recurrent co-usage patterns. It describes trace-to-tool links and three entry sets for affordances, boundaries, and co-usage.
regions.visible_text: Tool-Capability Graph. Agent-neutral traces make rollouts reusable, but they are still organized by task. To support tool-side capability discovery, ToolAtlas builds a Tool-Capability Graph G_cap whose nodes are tools and whose inter-tool edges summarize recurrent co-usage patterns observed in agent-neutral traces. A tool node is connected to every trace node whose agent-neutral trace uses that tool, and we denote these trace-tool links by E_trace↔tool. These links let the tool node gather what related trace nodes reveal about the tool. Each tool node t_i carries three entry sets (U_i, B_i, C_i), where affordance entries U_i record valid uses that t_i reliably supports, boundary entries B_i mark regimes where t_i becomes unreliable or infeasible, and co-usage entries C_i document recurrent compositions with peer tools.

regions.label: Operational-state explanation
regions.description: Observed: The paragraph explains that capability, boundary, and co-usage entries summarize the operational state used for later exploration.
regions.visible_text: This graph is the operational state used later for capability exploration. It tells the proposer what is already known about a tool and which affordances, boundaries, or compositions remain under-covered.

regions.label: Tool-Strategy Graph subsection text
regions.description: Observed: The prose says memory induction groups semantically related or structurally similar traces into strategy nodes and defines a Tool-Strategy Graph.
regions.visible_text: Tool-Strategy Graph. Some lessons are planning patterns rather than single-tool properties. Memory Induction captures them by grouping semantically related trace nodes or trace nodes with shared tool-use patterns, then distilling recurring task tips into strategy nodes. These nodes form the Tool-Strategy Graph G_strat = (V_strat, E_strat).

regions.label: Trace-strategy links and example
regions.description: Observed: The right-column continuation defines bidirectional trace-strategy links and gives a file-system example involving allowed directories and a writable workspace.
regions.visible_text: We denote bidirectional trace-strategy links by E_trace↔strat. For example, file-system traces that first check allowed directories and locate the writable workspace can induce a strategy to discover the workspace and target scope before acting. This graph lets a user agent reuse high-level plans on similar tasks.

regions.label: Complete tool-memory graph definition
regions.description: Observed: The paragraph states that after Memory Induction, the complete memory consists of trace, capability, and strategy graphs with cross-graph links.
regions.visible_text: After Memory Induction, the complete tool memory graph consists of the three graphs, M_T = (G_trace, G_cap, G_strat) with cross-graph links E_trace↔tool between trace nodes and supported tool nodes, and E_trace↔strat between trace nodes and supported strategy nodes.

regions.label: Section 3.2 heading
regions.description: Observed: Bold numbered section heading in the right column.

regions.label: Capability Exploration opening paragraph
regions.description: Observed: The section explains that seed tasks cover only a small portion of tool capability, so ToolAtlas expands memory using the Tool-Capability Graph as feedback and proposes tasks targeting uncertain areas.
regions.visible_text: Memory Bootstrapping gives the MCP service an initial tool-side memory, but seed tasks still cover only a small region of the tool capability. Capability Exploration expands M_T by using the Tool-Capability Graph as feedback. The graph records what is already known about each tool, and the task proposer uses that state to propose tasks that test what remains uncertain. At round r, ToolAtlas samples a local subgraph S^(r) of K related tools from the current Tool-Capability Graph G_cap^(r−1). The sampler starts from a target tool and follows co-usage edges, favoring plausible compositions.
